chapter.name: Describing Motion Around Us
chapter.blurb: Motion in a straight line is described using a reference point, distance travelled and displacement, average speed and average velocity (including a postmen problem from the historical Ganitakaumudi), and average acceleration, illustrated by a bus speeding up and braking and by a freely falling object introducing g. Position-time and velocity-time graphs are plotted and read, with slope giving velocity or acceleration and area under a velocity-time graph giving displacement. Three kinematic equations connect displacement, time, initial velocity, final velocity and acceleration for constant-acceleration motion, applied to braking-distance problems. The chapter ends with motion in a plane through uniform circular motion, where a constant speed but continuously changing direction still counts as accelerated motion.

scope_in.item: Position of an object described by its distance and direction from a fixed reference point; an object is in motion if this position changes with time, at rest if it does not

Distance travelled (total path length) versus displacement (net change in position, with direction); both measured in metres; magnitude of displacement is less than or equal to distance travelled, equal only when the object moves without reversing direction
Average speed = total distance travelled / time interval (magnitude only, no direction); uniform motion (equal distances in equal time intervals) versus non-uniform motion

Average velocity = displacement / time interval, with direction shown by + or - signs; average velocity as the average rate of change of position; for straight-line motion in one direction only, average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are equal

Average acceleration = change in velocity / time interval, SI unit m s-2; direction of average acceleration is with the velocity when speed is increasing and opposite to the velocity when speed is decreasing; acceleration due to gravity (g, about 9.8 m/s^2) as an example of constant acceleration
Plotting a position-time or velocity-time graph from a table of values: choosing axes and a scale, and joining the plotted points

Interpreting a position-time graph: straight line = constant velocity, line parallel to the time axis = object at rest, curve = non-uniform (accelerated) motion; finding average velocity from the slope of a position-time graph

Interpreting a velocity-time graph: line parallel to the time axis = constant velocity (zero acceleration), straight sloped line = constant acceleration; finding acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph; finding displacement from the area enclosed between the velocity-time graph and the time axis
The three kinematic equations for straight-line motion with constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, and using them to solve for an unknown quantity given the others

Motion in a plane (two dimensions) introduced through everyday examples; uniform circular motion: constant speed along a circular path, distance in one revolution = circumference (2 pi R), displacement after one full revolution = 0, average speed for one revolution = 2 pi R / T

In uniform circular motion, velocity at any point is directed along the tangent to the circle at that point; because the direction of velocity keeps changing continuously even though the speed is constant, uniform circular motion is accelerated motion

concepts.name: Describing position: reference point, motion and rest
concepts.description: The position of an object at any instant is described by its distance and direction from a chosen reference point; the object is in motion if this position changes with time and at rest if it does not.
concepts.idea: To say where something is, you need a fixed starting point to measure from, and both how far and which way the object is from it.
concepts.rule: To describe the position of an object, we first fix a reference point (also called the origin). The distance and direction of the object from this reference point, at any instant of time, describes its position at that instant. If the position of the object with respect to the reference point changes with time, the object is said to be in motion; if it does not change with time, the object is at rest. On a straight line, positions to one side of the reference point (commonly the right) are taken as positive and to the other side as negative.
concepts.example: An athlete starts running from a reference point O marked on a straight track; her positions at later instants are recorded as distances to the right (positive) or left (negative) of O.

questions.a: Yes; although the distance from the lamppost is the same (15 m) at both times, the direction has changed from right (+15 m) to left (-15 m), so her position relative to the reference point has changed.

questions.q: A fixed lamppost and a car moving alongside a cyclist at exactly the cyclist's speed are used, in turn, as reference points for describing the cyclist's motion. Analyse whether the cyclist is in motion using each reference point, and explain why the two answers differ.

questions.q: A classmate claims that an object can never truly be called 'at rest' because everything in the universe is moving in some sense. Do you agree, using the idea of a reference point? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned view either way is acceptable if justified; the stronger argument is that rest and motion are always defined with respect to a chosen reference point, so an object can correctly be called 'at rest' relative to a suitable reference point (e.g. the ground) even though it may be in motion relative to another (e.g. the Sun).
s: Reasoning using the reference point idea

questions.a: For example: place a toy on a slowly moving toy trolley on a table. concepts.name: Distance travelled and displacement
concepts.description: Distance travelled is the total length of the path covered by an object; displacement is the net change in position between two instants, with a direction, and its magnitude can never exceed the distance travelled.
concepts.idea: Distance is how much ground you covered in total; displacement is how far, and in which direction, you ended up from where you started.
concepts.rule: Distance travelled is the total length of the actual path covered by an object; it needs only a numerical value with units. Displacement is the net change in position of an object between two given instants of time; it needs both a numerical value (magnitude) and a direction. The SI unit for both is the metre (m). The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to the total distance travelled; they are equal only when the object moves without turning back, i.e. in one direction only.
concepts.example: An athlete runs from O up to A and back to B along the same straight track: the total distance travelled is the sum of all the path lengths covered, while the displacement is just the straight-line distance and direction from O to the final position.

questions.q: A hiker walks 3 km east, then 4 km north, ending at a point that is, in a straight line, 5 km from the start. Analyse: is the magnitude of her displacement equal to, less than, or greater than her total distance travelled, and explain your reasoning using the actual numbers.
questions.a: Total distance travelled = 3 km + 4 km = 7 km. Magnitude of displacement (the straight-line distance from start to end) = 5 km. Since 5 km is less than 7 km, the magnitude of displacement is less than the total distance travelled, which is expected because the hiker changed direction partway rather than travelling in one straight line.

questions.q: A classmate says that if two joggers cover the same distance in a park, they must also have the same displacement. Do you agree? Justify with an example.
questions.a: Disagree; two joggers can cover equal distances but along different paths or directions, ending at different points, so their displacements can differ even though their distances travelled are equal (for example, one jogs 400 m in a straight line while another jogs 400 m around a curved path back near the start).

The total distance travelled is 40 steps, but because the path returns exactly to the starting point, the net displacement is zero.

concepts.name: Average speed and average velocity
concepts.description: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time interval (a magnitude-only quantity); average velocity is the displacement divided by the time interval and includes direction; motion is uniform if equal distances are covered in equal time intervals.
concepts.idea: Speed tells you how fast without caring which way; velocity tells you how fast and which way.
concepts.rule: Average speed = total distance travelled / time interval; it has only a numerical value, no direction. Average velocity = displacement / time interval; its direction is the same as the direction of displacement, shown by a + or - sign. The SI unit of both is metre per second (m/s), also commonly km/h. For straight-line motion in one direction only, average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are equal. Motion is uniform if an object covers equal distances in equal time intervals (constant speed); otherwise it is non-uniform.
concepts.example: Sarang swims 25 m to the far end of a pool and 25 m back in 50 s: total distance = 50 m, so average speed = 1 m/s, but his displacement is 0 m, so his average velocity is 0 m/s.

questions.q: Explain why average speed can never be negative, while average velocity can be positive, negative or zero.

questions.q: A scooter travels 45 km in 1.5 hours in one direction along a straight road, without ever turning back. Find its average speed in km/h and its average velocity.
questions.a: Average speed = 45 km / 1.5 h = 30 km/h. Since the scooter never changes direction, displacement equals distance, so the average velocity is also 30 km/h in the direction of travel.
s: Average velocity = 30 km/h in the direction of travel

questions.q: A train covers 240 km east in 4 hours, halts, then returns 240 km west to its starting station in 4 hours. Find the average speed and average velocity for the entire 8-hour round trip.
questions.a: Total distance = 240 + 240 = 480 km, so average speed = 480 km / 8 h = 60 km/h. Total displacement = 0 km, since it returns to the start, so average velocity = 0 km/h.

questions.q: A jogger runs 900 m along a straight path in 6 minutes and then walks 300 m back along the same path in 4 minutes. What is her average speed for the whole 10-minute journey?
questions.a: 120 m/min

questions.q: A delivery van travels 100 km north in 2 hours, then 40 km south in 1 hour, on a straight highway. Find (i) its average speed, and (ii) its average velocity for the whole 3-hour trip, stating the direction of the velocity.
questions.a: (i) Total distance = 100 + 40 = 140 km, time = 3 h, so average speed = 140/3, about 46.7 km/h. (ii) Net displacement = 100 - 40 = 60 km north, so average velocity = 60 km / 3 h = 20 km/h north.

questions.q: Consider: (I) Average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity for the same journey. (II) Average speed can sometimes be less than the magnitude of average velocity for the same journey. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Compare the average speed and average velocity of a car that drives 50 km around a large circular route and ends exactly where it started, taking 1 hour.
questions.a: Its average speed is 50 km / 1 h = 50 km/h, a clear non-zero value, while its average velocity is 0 km/h because its net displacement is zero, since it returns to the starting point.

questions.q: A car's speedometer shows a steady 60 km/h throughout a 2-hour journey on a road that curves gently but never reverses direction, so the straight-line distance between the start and the end of the journey is only 90 km. Analyse whether the motion is uniform, and whether the average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity here, explaining any difference.
questions.a: Total distance travelled = 60 km/h x 2 h = 120 km, so average speed = 120 km / 2 h = 60 km/h, matching the steady speedometer reading, so the motion can be called uniform in speed. However, average velocity is based on displacement, which is only 90 km (the straight-line distance) here, so average velocity = 90 km / 2 h = 45 km/h, which is less than the average speed of 60 km/h. They differ because the road is curved, so displacement is shorter than the distance actually travelled.

questions.q: A student claims that a vehicle with a high average speed for a trip must also have a high average velocity. Do you agree? Justify your answer with reasoning.
questions.a: Disagree, in general; average speed depends only on total distance, while average velocity depends on displacement, so a vehicle that travels a long winding or looping path can have a high average speed but a low or even zero average velocity if it ends up close to its starting point.

questions.a: For example: the cyclist rides 2 km east to a customer, then 2 km west back to the shop, all within 20 minutes. The total distance travelled is 4 km, giving a clearly positive average speed of 4 km / (1/3 h) = 12 km/h, but because she ends exactly where she started, her net displacement is zero, making her average velocity zero.
s: Journey designed with distances and directions

concepts.name: Average acceleration
concepts.description: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval over which the change occurs; its direction depends on whether the object's speed is increasing or decreasing.
concepts.idea: Acceleration tells you how quickly velocity itself is changing, not how fast the object happens to be moving right now.
concepts.rule: Average acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time interval = (v - u) / t. Its SI unit is m/s^2 (m s-2). If the magnitude of velocity is increasing, the average acceleration is in the same direction as velocity; if the magnitude of velocity is decreasing, the average acceleration is opposite to the direction of velocity. This chapter considers only constant-acceleration motion, where velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals. Acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface (g, about 9.8 m/s^2) is an example of constant acceleration acting on a freely falling object.
concepts.example: A bus speeds up from 10 m/s to 15 m/s in 10 s (acceleration = 0.5 m/s^2, same direction as motion), then brakes from 15 m/s to rest in 5 s (acceleration = -3 m/s^2, opposite to the direction of motion).

A cyclist moving at 4 m/s along a straight road accelerates uniformly to 10 m/s in 3 s, and this acceleration stays constant. Find (i) the average acceleration during this interval, (ii) the cyclist's velocity 2 more seconds later (5 s after the start) if the same constant acceleration continued, and (iii) the direction of the acceleration.
questions.a: (i) Average acceleration = (10 - 4)/3 = 6/3 = 2 m/s^2. (ii) Since acceleration is constant, in 2 more seconds the velocity increases by 2 m/s^2 x 2 s = 4 m/s, so the velocity at 5 s = 10 + 4 = 14 m/s. (iii) Since speed increases throughout, the acceleration is in the same direction as the velocity (the direction of motion).

questions.q: Assertion (A): An object moving very fast can still have zero acceleration. Reason (R): acceleration depends on how quickly velocity is changing, not on how large the velocity is.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Compare the average acceleration of a bus speeding up from 10 m/s to 15 m/s in 10 s with that of the same bus later braking from 15 m/s to 0 m/s in 5 s, in terms of magnitude and direction.
questions.a: Speeding up: average acceleration = (15-10)/10 = 0.5 m/s^2, in the direction of velocity. Braking: average acceleration = (0-15)/5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to the direction of velocity. The braking acceleration has a much larger magnitude (3 m/s^2 vs 0.5 m/s^2) and acts opposite to the motion, while the speeding-up acceleration acts in the same direction as the motion.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from a height and its velocity increases by exactly 9.8 m/s in every successive one-second interval as it falls. Analyse: is this acceleration constant or changing, what is its value, and what would the ball's velocity be 3.5 s after being dropped (assuming it has not yet hit the ground)?
questions.a: Since the velocity increases by the same amount (9.8 m/s) in every successive one-second interval, the acceleration is constant, equal to g = 9.8 m/s^2, directed downward (the direction of motion). Using v = u + at with u = 0 m/s and t = 3.5 s, velocity = 0 + 9.8 x 3.5 = 34.3 m/s.

questions.q: A friend says that because a car is slowing down, its acceleration must be negative in every possible situation. Do you agree? Justify your answer using the direction convention discussed in the chapter.
questions.a: Not entirely; whether the acceleration is written as negative depends on which direction was chosen as positive. If the direction of the car's original motion is taken as positive, a slowing-down car does have a negative acceleration (since it is opposite to the velocity); but if the opposite direction had been chosen as positive, the same acceleration would be written as a positive number, so the sign is a matter of the convention chosen, not an absolute fact.

questions.q: Design a short scenario, different from the bus example in the chapter, describing an object whose average acceleration is exactly zero for part of its journey and non-zero for another part. Give the velocities and time intervals you choose, and identify which part has zero and which has non-zero acceleration.
questions.a: For example: a car travels at a constant 20 m/s for 10 s (acceleration = (20-20)/10 = 0 m/s^2, so zero acceleration in this part), then speeds up from 20 m/s to 30 m/s in the next 5 s (acceleration = (30-20)/5 = 2 m/s^2, a non-zero acceleration in this part).
s: Scenario designed with velocities and times
Correctly identifies the non-zero-acceleration part with its value

concepts.name: Position-time and velocity-time graphs
concepts.description: Position-time and velocity-time graphs show how position or velocity changes with time; the slope of a position-time graph gives velocity, the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
concepts.idea: A graph turns a table of numbers into a picture that shows, at a glance, whether motion is steady or changing.
concepts.rule: On a position-time graph, a straight line means constant velocity (uniform motion) and a curve means changing velocity (non-uniform, accelerated motion); a line parallel to the time axis means the object is at rest. Slope = (change in the quantity on the Y-axis) / (change in time). On a position-time graph, slope = average velocity. On a velocity-time graph, a line parallel to the time axis means constant velocity and zero acceleration; a straight sloped line means constant acceleration, and its slope gives that average acceleration; the area enclosed between the line and the time axis, for a given time interval, gives the displacement in that interval.
concepts.example: For a car whose velocity increases steadily from 0 to 15 m/s over 30 s, drawn as a straight sloped line, the slope of the line gives its average acceleration, and the area of the resulting triangle gives the total displacement.

questions.q: On a position-time graph, a straight line indicates that the object is moving with ____ velocity.
questions.a: constant

questions.q: On a position-time graph, a line parallel to the time axis represents an object that is
questions.a: at rest

questions.q: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the object's
questions.a: acceleration

questions.q: Which of these can NOT be found from a velocity-time graph?
questions.a: the exact route or path the object followed on the ground

the displacement, from the area under the graph
the velocity at any instant of time

questions.q: A curved (non-straight) position-time graph indicates that the object's motion is
questions.a: non-uniform (accelerated)

questions.q: The area enclosed between a velocity-time graph and the time axis, for a given time interval, gives the object's ____ in that interval.
questions.a: displacement

questions.q: A line parallel to the time axis on a velocity-time graph shows that the object's acceleration is
questions.a: zero

questions.q: Two objects' position-time graphs are straight lines through the origin, but one line is steeper than the other. What does the steeper line indicate?
questions.a: a higher velocity
o: the same velocity as the other line

questions.q: Explain why a straight, upward-sloping line on a velocity-time graph indicates constant acceleration rather than constant velocity.
questions.a: A straight line on a velocity-time graph means the slope (which represents acceleration, the rate of change of velocity) is the same throughout, so the acceleration is constant; the velocity itself is shown to be increasing steadily along the line, not staying the same, so it is the acceleration, not the velocity, that stays constant.
s: Slope of a velocity-time graph = acceleration
Straight line means constant slope, hence constant acceleration, while velocity itself changes

questions.q: A position-time graph is a straight line passing through the points (0 s, 0 m) and (5 s, 25 m). The object's velocity is
questions.a: 5 m/s

questions.q: A velocity-time graph is a straight line rising from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (4 s, 12 m/s). The acceleration shown is

A position-time graph shows a car at position 10 m at t = 2 s and at position 50 m at t = 6 s, joined by a straight line. Find the average velocity of the car for this interval using the slope method.
questions.a: Slope = (50 m - 10 m)/(6 s - 2 s) = 40 m / 4 s = 10 m/s, so the average velocity of the car is 10 m/s.
s: Correct slope setup (change in position over change in time)

questions.q: A velocity-time graph is a straight line showing a scooter's velocity rising from 6 m/s at t = 2 s to 18 m/s at t = 8 s. Find its average acceleration from the slope, and state its direction relative to the velocity.
questions.a: Slope = (18 - 6) m/s / (8 - 2) s = 12/6 = 2 m/s^2, so the average acceleration is 2 m/s^2. Since the velocity is increasing, the acceleration acts in the same direction as the velocity.

questions.q: A velocity-time graph is a horizontal line at 8 m/s from t = 0 s to t = 5 s. The displacement in this interval, found from the area under the graph, is

A velocity-time graph is a straight line starting at 4 m/s (t = 0 s) and rising steadily to 14 m/s at t = 10 s. Using the graph, find (i) the acceleration from the slope, (ii) the displacement in this interval using the area (a rectangle of height 4 m/s plus a triangle on top), and (iii) confirm your displacement using the average of the initial and final velocity multiplied by time.
questions.a: (i) Acceleration = (14-4)/10 = 1 m/s^2. (ii) Area = rectangle (4 m/s x 10 s = 40 m) + triangle (0.5 x 10 s x (14-4) m/s = 0.5 x 10 x 10 = 50 m), total displacement = 40 + 50 = 90 m. (iii) Average of initial and final velocity x time = (4+14)/2 x 10 = 9 x 10 = 90 m, which matches the area calculation.
s: Confirms using average-velocity method, matches 90 m

questions.q: Assertion (A): A steeper straight line on a position-time graph always means the object is accelerating. Reason (R): the slope of a position-time graph represents velocity, not acceleration.
questions.a: A is false but R is true
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Compare what a straight-line position-time graph and a straight, sloped velocity-time graph each tell you about an object's motion.
questions.a: A straight-line position-time graph tells you the object is moving with constant velocity, given directly by its slope; a straight, sloped velocity-time graph tells you the object's velocity is changing at a constant rate, i.e. it has constant, non-zero acceleration, given by its slope.
s: Meaning of a straight position-time line
Meaning of a straight, sloped velocity-time line

questions.q: Two cars, P and Q, start from the same point at the same time and both have straight-line position-time graphs, but Q's line is steeper than P's. Both cars' velocity-time graphs turn out to be horizontal lines, Q's at a greater height than P's. Analyse what this combination of graphs tells you about the two cars' accelerations and which car covers more distance in the same time interval.
questions.a: Both position-time graphs being straight lines, and both velocity-time graphs being horizontal, show that both cars move with constant velocity, so both have zero acceleration. Since Q's position-time line is steeper, Q has the larger constant velocity, so Q covers a greater distance than P in the same time interval; this matches Q's velocity-time line being horizontal at a greater height than P's.
s: Both cars have zero acceleration, with reasoning
Q has the greater velocity, with reasoning
Q covers more distance, conclusion consistent across both graphs

questions.q: A student says that a curved position-time graph is 'wrong' because a graph representing real motion should always be a straight line. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Disagree; a curved position-time graph is not wrong, it correctly represents an object whose velocity is changing with time (non-uniform or accelerated motion), which is a very common and realistic kind of motion, such as a vehicle speeding up from rest.
s: Correct reasoning about curved graphs representing real non-uniform motion

questions.q: Describe, stage by stage, a velocity-time graph for a scooter that starts at rest, speeds up steadily for the first 5 s, then moves at a constant velocity for the next 10 s, and finally slows down steadily to rest in the last 4 s. Identify, for each stage, whether the acceleration is positive, negative or zero.
questions.a: Stage 1 (0-5 s): the line rises steadily from 0, a straight upward-sloping segment, so acceleration is positive (constant). Stage 2 (5-15 s): the line is horizontal at the top speed reached, so acceleration is zero. Stage 3 (15-19 s): the line falls steadily back down to zero, a straight downward-sloping segment, so acceleration is negative (constant).

concepts.name: Kinematic equations for constant acceleration
concepts.description: For straight-line motion with constant acceleration, the quantities displacement (s), time (t), initial velocity (u), final velocity (v) and acceleration (a) are linked by three kinematic equations.
concepts.idea: When acceleration does not change, three simple equations let you find any one of these quantities if you know the others.
concepts.rule: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as. These equations are valid only when the acceleration is constant. A positive direction for the motion must be chosen and used consistently for u, v, a and s.
concepts.example: A car braking with a = -4 m/s^2 from an initial velocity of 15 m/s travels s = u^2 / 8 = 225/8 = 28.1 m before stopping, found using v^2 = u^2 + 2as with v = 0.

questions.q: The kinematic equation that gives final velocity in terms of initial velocity, acceleration and time is v = u + ____.
questions.a: at

questions.q: Which kinematic equation relates displacement directly to initial velocity, time and acceleration, without needing final velocity?
The three kinematic equations given in this chapter apply to motion in a straight line with
questions.a: constant acceleration

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three kinematic equations given in the chapter?
questions.a: s = v/t

questions.q: In the equation v = u + at, the symbol 'u' stands for
questions.a: initial velocity

questions.q: The kinematic equation v^2 = u^2 + 2as is useful for finding displacement or velocity when the ____ is not known or not needed.
questions.a: time

questions.q: Before applying any of the three kinematic equations to a straight-line motion problem, it must first be checked that the
questions.a: acceleration is constant throughout the motion
o: acceleration is constant throughout the motion

questions.q: A problem gives you the initial velocity, the acceleration and the time taken, and asks for the final velocity. Which equation should be used directly?
questions.a: v = u + at

questions.q: Explain why all three kinematic equations become invalid if an object's acceleration is changing during its motion.
questions.a: The three kinematic equations were derived assuming that acceleration stays constant throughout the interval considered, so that the acceleration at every instant equals the average acceleration over that interval; if the acceleration actually changes during the motion, this assumption fails and the equations no longer give correct results.
s: Assumption fails if acceleration changes, so equations become invalid

questions.q: A car starts at 5 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s^2 for 4 s. Using v = u + at, its final velocity is
questions.a: 13 m/s

questions.q: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 3 m/s^2 for 5 s. Using s = ut + (1/2)at^2, the distance it covers is
A cyclist moving at 6 m/s accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m/s^2 for 4 s. Find her final velocity, and the distance she covers in this time.
questions.a: Final velocity: v = u + at = 6 + 1.5 x 4 = 6 + 6 = 12 m/s. Distance: s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = 6x4 + 0.5x1.5x16 = 24 + 12 = 36 m.

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a constant acceleration of -5 m/s^2. Using v^2 = u^2 + 2as, find how far it travels before coming to rest.
A ball rolling at 2 m/s accelerates down a slope at 0.5 m/s^2 for 6 s. Using v = u + at, its velocity at the end is
questions.a: 5 m/s

questions.q: A motorbike moving at 24 m/s applies its brakes and comes to rest after travelling 72 m, with constant (negative) acceleration. Find (i) the acceleration using v^2 = u^2 + 2as, (ii) the time taken to stop using v = u + at, and (iii) verify your time using s = ut + (1/2)at^2.
questions.a: (i) 0 = 24^2 + 2a(72), so 0 = 576 + 144a, giving a = -4 m/s^2. (ii) 0 = 24 + (-4)t, giving t = 6 s. (iii) s = 24x6 + 0.5x(-4)x36 = 144 - 72 = 72 m, which matches the given distance, confirming the answers.
s: Verification using s = ut + (1/2)at^2 gives 72 m, matches

questions.q: Assertion (A): The equation v^2 = u^2 + 2as can be used to find the displacement of a braking car even if the exact time taken to stop is unknown. Reason (R): this kinematic equation does not contain the time (t) at all.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A student is given initial velocity, final velocity and acceleration, and asked to find both the time taken and the displacement. Compare which of the three kinematic equations is the most direct choice for each quantity, and why.
questions.a: For time, v = u + at is the most direct choice, since it can be rearranged to t = (v-u)/a using only the three known quantities. For displacement, v^2 = u^2 + 2as is the most direct choice, since it relates s directly to u, v and a without needing t at all.
s: Time: v = u + at is direct, with reason
Displacement: v^2 = u^2 + 2as is direct, with reason

questions.q: A train accelerates uniformly from 15 m/s to 25 m/s while covering 200 m. Analyse this situation by finding (i) its acceleration using v^2 = u^2 + 2as, and (ii) the time it took, using two different kinematic equations, confirming both methods agree.
questions.a: (i) 25^2 = 15^2 + 2a(200), so 625 = 225 + 400a, giving a = 1 m/s^2. (ii) Method 1, v = u + at: 25 = 15 + 1xt, giving t = 10 s. Method 2, s = ut + (1/2)at^2: 200 = 15t + 0.5(1)t^2; substituting t = 10, 15(10) + 0.5(100) = 150 + 50 = 200, which matches, so both methods agree that t = 10 s.
s: Time found by v = u + at, t = 10 s
Confirmed using s = ut + (1/2)at^2, both methods agree

questions.q: A classmate insists that the equation v = u + at is enough to solve every problem in this chapter, and the other two kinematic equations are unnecessary. Do you agree? Justify your view.
questions.a: Disagree; while v = u + at is useful whenever time is known or wanted, many problems either do not give the time directly (better solved with v^2 = u^2 + 2as) or ask for displacement together with time (better solved with s = ut + (1/2)at^2), so having all three equations lets you choose the most direct method depending on which quantities are known.
s: Justification referencing the other equations' uses

questions.q: Design your own straight-line motion word problem, with your own numbers for two known quantities among u, v, a, t, s (not including time), that requires the third kinematic equation, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, to solve for a missing quantity. State the problem, solve it, and show your working.
questions.a: For example: 'A skateboarder moving at 8 m/s accelerates down a ramp at 2 m/s^2 over a distance of 15 m. Find her final velocity.' Using v^2 = u^2 + 2as: v^2 = 8^2 + 2x2x15 = 64+60 = 124, so v is the square root of 124, about 11.1 m/s.
s: Original problem designed using u, a, s without given time
Correct final answer with working shown

concepts.name: Motion in a plane: uniform circular motion
concepts.description: Uniform circular motion is motion along a circular path at constant speed; even though speed stays constant, the direction of velocity keeps changing continuously, so the motion is accelerated.
concepts.idea: Going around and around at a steady pace still counts as accelerating, because acceleration cares about direction too, not just speed.
concepts.rule: Distance travelled in one revolution = circumference of the circle = 2 pi R; displacement after one full revolution = 0 (the object returns to the start); average speed for one revolution = 2 pi R / T, where T is the time period. In uniform circular motion, the velocity at any point is directed along the tangent to the circle at that point, in the direction of motion. Because this direction keeps changing continuously even though the speed is constant, uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.
concepts.example: A child on a merry-go-round moving from A to B to C: the distance travelled is the curved path ABC, while the displacement is the straight line from A to C, which would become zero after a full revolution back to A.

questions.q: Motion of an object along a circular path with constant speed is called ____ circular motion.
questions.a: uniform

questions.q: The distance travelled by an object in one complete revolution of a circle of radius R is
questions.a: 2 pi R

questions.q: After completing exactly one full revolution of a circular path, an object's displacement from its starting point is
questions.a: zero

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of uniform circular motion?
questions.a: the direction of velocity stays fixed throughout the motion
o: the direction of velocity stays fixed throughout the motion
the speed is constant throughout the motion
the velocity is directed along the tangent to the circle
the motion is accelerated even though the speed does not change

questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the velocity at any point on the circle is directed
questions.a: along the tangent to the circle at that point
o: along the tangent to the circle at that point
along the radius, towards the centre
along the radius, away from the centre
opposite to the direction of motion

questions.q: The average speed for one revolution of an object moving in a circle of radius R and time period T is given by 2 pi R divided by ____.
questions.a: T

questions.q: Uniform circular motion is described as accelerated motion mainly because
questions.a: the direction of velocity is continuously changing
o: the direction of velocity is continuously changing

questions.q: A child on a merry-go-round completes exactly half a revolution, ending diametrically opposite her starting point. Compared to the distance she travelled, her displacement is
questions.a: less than the distance travelled, and equal to the diameter of the circle
o: less than the distance travelled, and equal to the diameter of the circle

questions.q: Explain why an object moving in uniform circular motion is accelerating even though its speed never changes.
questions.a: Acceleration depends on the change in velocity, and velocity includes direction as well as magnitude (speed); in uniform circular motion, the speed stays the same but the direction of the velocity keeps changing continuously as the object goes around the circle, so the velocity is changing, which means the object is accelerating.
s: Direction keeps changing even though speed is constant, so acceleration is present

questions.q: A toy train moves once around a circular track of radius 7 m. Taking pi = 22/7, the distance it travels in this one revolution is
An object completes one revolution of a circular path of radius 7 m in 22 s. Taking pi = 22/7, its average speed is
questions.a: 2 m/s

questions.q: A model satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 14 m and takes 44 s to complete one revolution. Taking pi = 22/7, find (i) the distance travelled in one revolution, and (ii) its average speed.
questions.a: (i) Distance = 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 2 x 44 = 88 m. (ii) Average speed = 88 m / 44 s = 2 m/s.

questions.q: A cyclist rides once around a circular park of radius 21 m, taking pi = 22/7, and returns to her exact starting point. Find (i) the distance she travelled, and (ii) her displacement, explaining your answer for (ii).
questions.a: (i) Distance = 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 2 x 66 = 132 m. (ii) Displacement = 0 m, because she returns to exactly the same starting point after one complete revolution.

questions.q: A horse on a merry-go-round moves along a circular path of radius 3.5 m and completes one revolution in 11 s. Taking pi = 22/7, its average speed is
questions.a: 2 m/s

questions.q: A point on the rim of a wheel of radius 0.7 m completes 5 revolutions in 22 s. Taking pi = 22/7, find (i) the distance travelled by the point in these 5 revolutions, (ii) its displacement at the end of the 5 revolutions, and (iii) its average speed over this time.
questions.a: (i) Distance in 1 revolution = 2 x 22/7 x 0.7 = 4.4 m; in 5 revolutions = 5 x 4.4 = 22 m. (ii) Since 5 is a whole number of revolutions, the point returns exactly to its starting point, so displacement = 0 m. (iii) Average speed = total distance/time = 22 m / 22 s = 1 m/s.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In uniform circular motion, the magnitude of the object's velocity is constantly changing. Reason (R): in uniform circular motion, the speed of the object stays constant, but its direction keeps changing.
questions.a: A is false but R is true
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Compare the distance travelled and displacement of a child on a merry-go-round after (i) one quarter of a revolution and (ii) one complete revolution.
questions.a: After one quarter revolution, the distance travelled is one quarter of the circumference (a non-zero curved-path length), while the displacement is the shorter, straight-line distance between the start and the quarter-way point, which is non-zero but less than that quarter-circumference. After one complete revolution, the distance travelled is the full circumference (non-zero), while the displacement is zero because the child returns to the exact starting point.
s: Quarter revolution: distance and displacement both non-zero, displacement shorter
Full revolution: distance non-zero, displacement zero

questions.q: An athlete runs along a square track and another runs along a circular track of the same perimeter, both at constant speed. Analyse how many times each athlete's direction of velocity changes in one full lap, and which of the two is undergoing acceleration throughout the entire lap, explaining why.
questions.a: On the square track, the athlete's direction changes abruptly four times, once at each corner, and stays constant along each straight side, so this athlete accelerates only briefly at the four corners, not throughout the lap. On the circular track, the direction of velocity changes continuously at every point of the path, since the track has no straight sections, so this athlete is accelerating throughout the entire lap, even though the speed is constant in both cases.
s: Square track: direction changes only at the 4 corners
Correct conclusion: circular-track athlete accelerates throughout, with reasoning

questions.q: A classmate argues that because a car going around a circular roundabout shows a constant reading on its speedometer, it cannot be accelerating. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Disagree; the speedometer only shows the magnitude of velocity (speed), but acceleration depends on velocity, which includes direction as well; since the car's direction is continuously changing as it goes around the roundabout even at a constant speedometer reading, the car is accelerating.
s: Reasoning distinguishing speed and velocity direction

questions.q: Design a simple real-life example, different from the merry-go-round, a satellite, or a wheel already used in the chapter, of an object undergoing uniform circular motion. Describe its circular path and explain, using the idea of changing direction, why it is accelerating even at constant speed.
questions.a: For example: the tip of a clock's second hand moving around the clock face at a constant rate. It moves along a circular path of radius equal to the hand's length, covering the full circle every 60 seconds at constant speed. Even though its speed never changes, the direction in which the tip is moving keeps changing continuously as it goes around, so its velocity is continuously changing, meaning the tip is constantly accelerating.
s: Original example described with a circular path
Explains acceleration via continuously changing direction
